entities.name: Arab Nationalist Movement
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Arab Nationalist Movement (ANM, حركة القوميين العرب, Harakat al-Qawmiyyin al-Arab), founded in 1951 at the American University of Beirut by George Habash (a Palestinian Christian), Wadi' Haddad, and others — was one of the most significant pan-Arab political movements of the 1950s-1970s, beginning as an idealistic student movement committed to Arab unity and Palestinian liberation and evolving into a radicalized militant organization that pioneered international airplane hijacking and became a significant actor in Cold War terrorism.

George Habash's ANM was founded in the immediate aftermath of the 1948 Arab-Israeli War and the Nakba (Palestinian Catastrophe), in which approximately 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homeland. This founding trauma shaped the ANM's ideology: unlike the Ba'ath Party's focus on state-level Arab nationalism, the ANM focused on pan-Arab unity as the prerequisite for Palestinian liberation, arguing that only a unified Arab world could defeat Israel.

The ANM's evolution from student movement to militant organization reflects the radicalization of Palestinian politics after successive Arab defeats: after the catastrophic 1967 Six-Day War destroyed the pan-Arab project, the ANM reconstituted as the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which under Wadi' Haddad pioneered airplane hijacking as a political tactic — a tactical innovation that transformed global terrorism and counter-terrorism. George Habash and the PFLP's 1968-1972 airplane hijacking campaign permanently changed international aviation security.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Arab Nationalist Movement — founded after the 1948 Nakba, evolving into the PFLP that pioneered international airplane hijacking, permanently transforming global aviation security — is historically significant as a monument to Palestinian political radicalization and the origins of modern international terrorism.
